The United States abandoned the gold standard in March and April 1933, when President Franklin D. Roosevelt took several actions to halt the hoarding of gold and devalue the dollar [3][5]. Specifically, the government mandated the exchange of gold coinage for dollars and ended the use of gold as legal tender for debts [5]. This action allowed the dollar to float freely on foreign exchange markets without a fixed price in gold [5].

The end of Roman rule in Britain was marked by the expulsion of Roman officials by the Romano-British people around 410 AD [1][2]. Different theories exist regarding the exact sequence of events, but it is clear that the Romano-British took charge of their own affairs when they expelled the Roman officials and requested assistance from Rome, which was not forthcoming [1][2]. The historian Michael Jones suggested that the Britons first appealed to Rome and only expelled the Roman officials when they received no help [2]. Theodor Mommsen argued that it was Rome that gave up Britain due to other priorities [5].

In networking, NAT stands for Network Address Translation [1][2]. It is a method of remapping one IP address space into another by modifying network address information in the IP header of packets while they are in transit across a traffic routing device [1][2]. NAT was originally used to avoid the need to readdress every host when a network was moved, but it has become a popular tool to conserve global address space in the face of IPv4 address exhaustion [1]. NAT allows a single IP address to represent an entire private network, hiding the IP addresses of multiple hosts behind a single public IP address [3].
